messages.subject: matrix vector multiplication with diag_matrix
parts:
So I've pulled stan from git and have been playing around with specifying a time series model.  I've run into an issue and I'm not sure if it's a bug or if I'm just doing something silly.

It's a simple AR model and the specification has the line:

lambda[t] ~ multi_normal( diag_matrix(1-phi)*mu + diag_matrix(phi)*lambda[t-1], U );

where lambda, phi and mu are vectors and U is a cov_matrix.

The parser chokes with:

lambda[t] ~ multi_normal( diag_matrix(1-phi)*mu + diag_matrix(phi)*lambda[t-1], U );
                                                               ^-- here

DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:

expression is ill formed
Parser expecting: <eps>


Any suggestions?  I've tried a number of different variations on the expression, including defining transformed variables to represent the mean to no avail.

Also, on a related note, has anyone created a time-series demo for stan?  If not I'd be more than happy to contribute this one once I get it running.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] matrix vector multiplication with diag_matrix
parts:
This discussion should also probably be on
stan-users, not that it's had any traffic yet.

I really need to write some doc! And work on some
better parser error messages.

The basic problem is that Stan's not very sophisticated
about the syntax for matrices. All the operations need
to be spelled out Lisp-like (I plan to add better parsing
for them at some point).

The expression for matrix product is "multiply(x,y)".
You can see the available ops in src/stan/math/matrix.hpp and
src/stan/agrad/matrix.hpp.

> lambda[t] ~ multi_normal( diag_matrix(1-phi)*mu +
> diag_matrix(phi)*lambda[t-1], U );
>
> where lambda, phi and mu are vectors and U is a cov_matrix.

To get (phi - 1), you need to either create a unit
vector one and use "minus(phi,one)", or write it
out longhand (which is just as fast as everything's
automatically "vectorized" when the generated code gets
compiled). For instance, you can do phi-1 this way if
phi is a parameter:

transformed parameters {
vector(K) phi_m_1; // K should be sample size
for (k in 1:K) phi_m_1[k] <- phi[k] - 1;

}

The same goes for the other matrix ops.

We've been working on some time-series data on
the side. But nothing's been contributed. We'll
set up some way to let people contribute models and
data so other people can run them. I think it'd
be a great resource.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] matrix vector multiplication with diag_matrix
parts:
No, we're not trying to be consistent with BUGS
or with JAGS (which aren't themselves consistent
with each other).

Our variables are typed. We have many more special
fucntions. We don't have the same parameterizations
of densities. We allow improper priors. We allow
direct manipulation of the total log probability
function so you can define your own densities or
transformations of existing densities (with Jacobian
determinants).

To be consistent with JAGS, we'd also need to use the funky
"%*%" notation for matrix operators, whereas I'm just
going to overload "*", etc.

We're behind in not having all the cumulative
densities (yet) and not having all the random generation
functions (again, as of yet). Those, we plan to add
as we go along.

- Bob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: function and operator names and syntax
parts:
Maybe we can call our currently function syntax
Python-like (or is that really numpy-like?)
and be done with it.

Seriously, though, I haven't at all been concerned
with compatibility with anything existing. I've tried to
be internally consistent, but we could use some review.

I went with full versions of distribution names,
like normal(0,1), instead of norm(0,1) or R/BUGS/JAGS
dnorm(0,1). And our parameterization uses scale, not
precision or squared scale.

I suppose we could add a precision-parameterized

normal(mu,tau)

and then add a scale-parameterized version,

normal_scale(mu,sigma);

and one with squared scale (aka variance), as in:

normal_squared_scale(mu,sigma_sq);

We also have the Cholesky-factor parameterization in the
multivariate case.

There are no element-wise ops, at least not yet. I've
reduced results where possible. So there are ops like:

double multiply(row_vector,vector);

matrix multiply(vector,row_vector);

But there are NO element-wise ops like:

vector multiply(vector,vector);

Should we add elementwise ops? And what should they be
called?

Does JAGS have element-wise ops? If I do (v1 * v2),
is that interpreted element-wise? Is that why they use the
funny %*% notation for matrix ops? I didn't see it in their
doc (I could've missed it or it could just not be in the doc).

I haven't implemented dim(matrix), so no:

vector<int> dim(matrix);

On the other hand, there are generic dot products,

double dot_product(vector,vector);
double dot_product(row_vector,vector);

but I spelled the name out in full.

We're also not allowing the left-hand-side assignment
algebra, as in:

logit(theta) <- x

and instead require:

theta <- inv_logit(x)


We just have to make up our minds before I start the doc
process.

- Bob

> I suppose we could add a precision-parameterized
>
> normal(mu,tau)

I think the default should be the scale-parameterized version (as in R). I say that even though I use the variance-parameterized version in BDA. I do not not not not not want the so-called precision-parameterized version to be the default. But I agree that it would be ok to have alternative forms.

The alternative forms will be particularly important for inverse-chi^s dist and negative-binomial ("overdispersed Poisson").

Personally, I'm happy with the R convention that +, -, *, / operate component-wise. I find that to be very convenient. But if it's confusing, we don't need it.

>

> is that interpreted element-wise? Is that why they use the
> funny %*% notation for matrix ops? I didn't see it in their
> doc (I could've missed it or it could just not be in the doc).

Again, I don't see the point of being Jags-compliant, I'd prefer to be consistent with R or Matlab or Python or whatever.

>
> vector<int> dim(matrix);
>
> On the other hand, there are generic dot products,
>
> double dot_product(vector,vector);
> double dot_product(row_vector,vector);
>

>
> We're also not allowing the left-hand-side assignment
> algebra, as in:
>
> logit(theta) <- x
>
> and instead require:
>
> theta <- inv_logit(x)

That's fine with me. I've never liked the "logit(theta) <- x" notation. This relates to my desire for our code to be executable code rather than just an interpreted model. One thing that I found difficult about Bugs is that its model is _not_ actually code that runs in order. Also, in my books I used the invlogit notation. (I actually call it invlogit() in R, but if you prefer inv_logit, that's fine. Some people write expit, which makes logical sense but I've never used it, as it seems like just one more thing to learn.

The latter is the standard convention in mathematical typesetting
